outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundational context of the dispute, identifying the parties involved (Finesse vs. AT&T/Nokia), the subject matter technology (Passive Intermodulation Product cancellation in wireless radios), and the specific patents at issue ('134 and '775). It details the procedural history from the initial lawsuit in the Eastern District of Texas, through the jury verdict finding validity and infringement with a significant damages award, to the post-trial motions for Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL) regarding non-infringement and damages. Finally, it outlines the current appeal status before the Federal Circuit.

Patent Claims Asserted: Summary of '134 and '775 Patents
Procedural History: Trial Verdict and Jury Findings

Jurisdictional Basis for Appeal

outline.chapter_title: Standard of Review and Legal Framework for JMOL
outline.description: Before analyzing the merits, this chapter defines the appellate court's role. It explains that although this is a Federal Circuit case involving patent law, the standard for reviewing a denial of JMOL follows the local circuit law (Fifth Circuit) due to venue. It clarifies the distinction between reviewing claim construction (de novo) versus factual findings regarding infringement (substantial evidence). Crucially, it sets forth the rigorous standard required to overturn a jury verdict via JMOL: evidence must point so overwhelmingly to one side that no reasonable juror could reach a contrary conclusion.
subtopics: De Novo Review Standard for Denials of JMOL (Fifth Circuit Law)
'Substantial Evidence' Threshold for Jury Verdicts
Review Standards for Claim Construction vs. Factual Findings
Burden of Proof on Plaintiff Regarding Claim Limitations

outline.chapter_title: '134 Patent Analysis: Insufficiency of Expert Testimony on Sampling Signals
outline.description: This chapter focuses on Claim 1 of the '134 patent, specifically limitation 1[a], which requires over-sampling a passband containing both "signals of interest" and "interference generating signals." It analyzes why Finesse failed to meet its burden despite having an expert witness. The core conflict lies in Dr. Wells' testimony mapping these terms to diagram elements labeled "downlink TX reference" and "modeled PIM path," while simultaneously acknowledging that modeling happens *after* sampling. The court finds Dr. Wells' testimony self-contradictory and ambiguous regarding whether physical signals exist at the moment of sampling, rendering it legally insufficient to support a jury verdict.
subtopics: '134 Patent Claim 1 Structure: Over-Sampling Requirement
Expert Witness Testimony Mapping Diagram Elements to Claim Terms

[Conclusion]: Reversal Due to Lack of Substantial Evidence for Limitation 1[a]

outline.chapter_title: '775 Patent Analysis: Failure to Prove Seven Distinct Multiplications
outline.description: This chapter examines Claim 1 of the '775 patent, focusing on limitations requiring three separately identifiable signals (not necessarily unique) multiplied in seven specific combinations. First, it addresses Appellants' argument regarding Prosecution History Estoppel; however, the court rejects this as there was no clear disavowal of two-input systems. Second, it analyzes why infringement fails regardless: Dr. Wells relied on documentation showing only three distinct multiplication types (using modulus/conjugates), failing to demonstrate how these covered all seven claimed mathematical operations ($S_1 	imes S_1 	imes S_2$, etc.). The lack of a direct mapping between documented operations and claimed steps means no reasonable jury could find infringement.

Prosecution History Estoppel Argument Dismissed

[Conclusion]: Reversal Due to Absence of Evidence for Seven-Multiplication Step

outline.description: This final chapter explains why an award previously upheld by a lower court is now voided without remand for retrial on damages alone. Since the Federal Circuit reversed *all* grounds for infringement across both patents due to lack of substantial evidence, there is no longer any valid basis upon which damages were calculated or assessed. Consequently, denying a new trial on damages becomes moot because there is no liability left to attach monetary value against.
subtopics: Relationship Between Liability Determination and Damage Awards
Mootness Principle Applied Here
Vacatur as Remedy Following Complete Reversal
